recipes.hook: Chest-up face + bold top-third hook text for 1.5–2.5s, then hard cut to screen record
recipes.mid: Screen record on the exact settings path; Remotion stat on the receipt number

recipes.hook: Face close-up, no text first second — emotion sells; stat pops at payoff phrase
recipes.mid: Mostly face; optional single UI screenshot as proof

recipes.when: Tool install / step process (Part X series style)
recipes.hook: Face + series hook text box at top; transition to full-screen UI early
recipes.mid: Continuous screen record with minimal face return
remotion: step labels optional — prefer native UI

prompt_rules: 9:16 product UI or terminal — not abstract AI brain
Lower third clear for face overlay if hook is split
Name the exact tool (Cursor, Claude Code, etc.)

anti_patterns: Avoid over-reliance on on-screen captions; this reel leans heavily on text, which can feel text-heavy for short-form
Avoid slow pacing if targeting global/fast-scroll audiences; 11s-per-shot is meditative but may lose impatient viewers
Avoid minimal branding/watermark presence; creator relies on face recognition rather than logo lock
Overly stylized animated brain graphics can read cheesy if not paired with serious voiceover—balance abstract AI visuals with grounded face time
Hindi/Urdu voiceover + Hindi/English mixed captions create friction for global audience; Jugal's English-first strategy may need subtitle clarity
Talking-head fatigue: 5+ frames of face risks scroll-past; lab footage saves it, but short-form needs 2-3 more visual breaks
Don't over-animate the screen swaps—static hard cuts feel more professional and credible than flashy transitions in educational content
Avoid cluttering the face with too many overlays; here, the 2 card PIPs work because they're clean, boxed, and placed in safe corners
Don't use generic stock music or B-roll; the face + named tools + branded UI is the payload—anything flashy dilutes authority
Over-reliance on one static shot; even slow-paced educational content benefits from subtle angle/framing shifts or cutaways
Minimal personality/humor in tone — this works for some audiences but risks losing Gen-Z viewers accustomed to faster, more irreverent ed-tech (e.g., MoocLab, @lex_fridman style)
No CTA or retention loop visible — 'watch till the end' in caption but no preview of payoff; could add teaser frame or end-screen element
Avoid heavy emoji or sticker overlays that compete with on-screen UI clarity — this works because graphics are minimal and intentional
Avoid rapid montage or jump-cuts; the slow deliberate pacing relies on creator credibility, not editing flashiness
Avoid music-driven beat-matching; this narrator-forward format needs clean audio focus
Avoid rapid montage or jump-cuts; this creator's strength is *clarity*, not hype—slow, methodical walkthrough fits the educational tone
Avoid heavy emoji or animated stickers on the talking-head portions—keeps the focus on facial expression and the hack itself
Avoid loud background music or dramatic sound design; the value is in the words and visuals, not production theater
Avoid standing lecture feel—Harper succeeds because she's warm and eye-contacting; don't default to voice-over + broll
Don't overload text density; this thrives on 4-6 word captions (not full sentences)
